threats.title: Unauthenticated submitter identity allows invoice impersonation
threats.rationale: The documentation states that the submitter is taken from a field in the uploaded invoice JSON and that submitters are not otherwise authenticated to the workflow: "The submitter field is a value in the uploaded document; submitters are not otherwise authenticated to the workflow." This means anyone with access to the submission channel can claim to be any approved submitter, enabling fraudulent invoices to be presented as coming from trusted parties.

threats.title: Prompt injection via invoice content and follow-up messages
threats.rationale: User-controlled content includes both the invoice JSON and conversational follow-up messages that ask the agent to reconsider denials and emphasize urgency: "Users submit an invoice as a text file containing a JSON document" and later "a note that the invoice is urgent and should be approved, asking the agent to reconsider its criteria. The agent's prior messages are carried into that follow-up." The agent is instructed to "use its best discretion" between deny and approve rules. No controls are described to treat this content as untrusted or to harden prompts, making the decision policy vulnerable to prompt-injection or policy-evasion attempts embedded in invoice fields or follow-up messages.

threats.title: Invoice contents exposed in observability traces
threats.rationale: The system sends detailed traces, including HTTP request and response bodies, to an external observability service: "Request and tool-call traces, including HTTP request and response bodies, are captured for debugging." Given that invoices are submitted as JSON documents and processed via tools, those bodies will routinely contain invoice contents (amount, submitter, category, due date) and possibly other metadata. This creates a risk that sensitive financial information is broadly accessible within the observability platform or retained longer than intended.

threats.title: Unclear data handling and access control at hosted model provider
threats.rationale: The agent is "backed by a hosted model provider" and "The invoice file's contents are parsed and returned to the model as the invoice details." While this documents that invoice data is sent to an external processor, there is no documented information about how the model provider stores, protects, or uses that data (e.g., training, retention, access controls, geographic location). This uncertainty is a material threat for compliance and confidentiality of customer invoice data.

threats.title: Policy override risk from urgent follow-up workflow
threats.rationale: If an invoice is denied, the workflow always follows up with a message stating that the invoice is urgent and should be approved, asking the agent to reconsider, and carrying prior messages into that conversation. The instructions also tell the agent to "use its best discretion" between deny and approve rules. This design creates a risk that the agent will override deny criteria under conversational pressure, weakening enforcement of the stated decision policy and potentially allowing high-value or non-approved invoices to be approved.

findings.title: Full HTTP request and response bodies, including invoice contents, are logged to the observability service
findings.rationale: The documentation explicitly states that request and tool-call traces include HTTP request and response bodies and are sent to an observability service. In this system, those HTTP bodies will routinely contain user-submitted invoice JSON (amount, submitter, category, due date) and tool results. This means invoice contents are written into logs/traces rather than being kept out of them. This is an inferred (high-confidence) violation of the requirement to keep sensitive data out of application logs, based on the combination of the system’s purpose (processing invoices) and the explicit logging of full HTTP bodies.
findings.evidence_quote:
"Users submit an invoice as a text file containing a JSON document. The agent is prompted with the path to the submitted file, reads it through its invoice-processing tool, and responds with the invoice details, an approve or deny decision, and the reasoning behind it."
...
"The invoice file's contents are parsed and returned to the model as the invoice details."
...
"Request and tool-call traces, including HTTP request and response bodies, are captured for debugging."

documentation_gaps.what_cannot_be_determined: Whether invoice contents and conversational follow-up messages are treated as untrusted model input (e.g., through prompt hardening, content filtering, or isolation) to mitigate prompt-injection and policy-evasion risks.
Whether the model’s approve/deny decisions and reasoning are validated or constrained by non-LLM logic or policy enforcement before being used to drive real-world payment actions.
Whether the data sent to the hosted model provider is minimized to only the fields necessary for decision-making, or whether additional invoice or workflow metadata is also transmitted.

How the model output (invoice details, approve/deny decision, reasoning) is encoded and rendered in any user interface or downstream system, and whether appropriate output encoding is applied to prevent injection into that context.
What privileged administrative capabilities exist (e.g., changing approval rules, tool configuration, credentials) and how access to those capabilities is restricted, authenticated, and documented.

How (or whether) users authenticate to the invoice submission workflow itself (distinct from the submitter field in the JSON) and whether any authentication is delegated to an identity provider with documented behavior.
Whether multi-factor authentication is required or supported for users who can submit invoices or otherwise influence financial approvals, and if so, who is responsible for enforcing it.
Whether the system is single-tenant or multi-tenant and, if multi-tenant, how tenant-aware authorization is enforced and documented for invoice data, logs, and decisions.

What privileges are granted to internal tools and external integrations (hosted model provider, observability service) and whether these privileges are limited strictly to what is required (least privilege).
The deployment pipeline for the agent (build, test, deploy steps), which components it depends on, and how the integrity and trustworthiness of that path are ensured.
Whether invoice files, derived invoice objects, and observability traces are encrypted in transit and at rest, including on the hosted model provider and observability service.
The defined retention periods for invoice submissions, derived data, and observability traces, and whether these retention practices are aligned with what customers are told.
If the service hosts multiple customers, whether stored artifacts (invoice files, derived objects, traces) are logically or physically separated by tenant.
Whether and how customer invoice data and associated traces can be deleted on request, including propagation of deletions to the hosted model provider and observability service.
Whether security-relevant administrative and financial actions (e.g., rule changes, credential updates, manual overrides) are recorded in logs or audit trails.

The network architecture and controls restricting reachability of internal components (agent runtime, tools) and access to external services (model provider, observability) to only the workloads that require them.
How the credentials for the model provider and observability service are stored, protected, and rotated, and whether a managed secret store is used.

The hosted model provider’s documented handling of invoice data (encryption, retention, training use, access controls, geographic location, and onward sharing) and how this is communicated to customers.
The observability service’s documented handling of traces that include invoice-related HTTP bodies (encryption, retention, access controls, data residency) and how this is communicated to customers.

questions.question: How do users authenticate to the invoice submission workflow, if at all? Is authentication delegated to an identity provider (e.g., SSO), and is that delegation documented?

What measures are in place to treat invoice contents and conversational follow-up messages as untrusted model input (e.g., prompt hardening, input filtering, or isolation) to mitigate prompt-injection and policy-evasion attacks?
Are the agent’s approve/deny decisions and reasoning validated or constrained by non-LLM logic or a policy engine before being used to trigger or authorize payments?
Can the invoice data sent to the hosted model provider be minimized to only the fields strictly necessary for decision-making, and is such minimization implemented today?
What encryption mechanisms are used for invoice data and traces in transit and at rest, including connections to and storage within the hosted model provider and observability service?
What are the retention periods for invoice submissions, derived invoice objects, and observability traces, and can these periods be configured or shortened per customer commitments?
Where and how are the model provider and observability service credentials stored (e.g., managed secret store), and what is the process for rotating and auditing these credentials?
What administrative interfaces exist to configure the agent (decision rules, tools, credentials), who has access to them, and how is privileged administrative access controlled and logged?

What documented data handling commitments (encryption, retention, training usage, geographic location, access controls) exist for the hosted model provider and observability service, and are these made available to customers?
Which security-relevant administrative or financial actions (e.g., rule changes, overrides, credential updates) are logged, and where are those logs stored and reviewed?
